# The Coins Example

Coins provide the simplest complete example of R<sup>2</sup>D.

Not because physical coin tossing is fundamental.

And not because R<sup>2</sup>D assumes probability.

The coins are useful because their possible states can be counted exactly.

That lets us separate four things that are easily confused:

- possible structure;
- realized occurrence;
- recursive replacement;
- and enclosing compatibility.

No energy is required.

No force is required.

No probability is required.

No physical trajectory is required.

No space or time is required.

The construction is finite combinatorics.

> **The coins do not model the mechanics of nature.  
> They expose the counting architecture.**

# Three Boundaries

Use three adjacent count levels:

$$
B_{n-1},
\qquad
B_n,
\qquad
B_{n+1}.
$$

At \(B_{n-1}\), the object is one coin.

At \(B_n\), the object is an ensemble of ten coins.

At \(B_{n+1}\), the object is an enclosing system containing ten such
ten-coin landscapes.

The recursion is

$$
\boxed{
10\times B_{n-1}
\longrightarrow
B_n
}
$$

followed by

$$
\boxed{
10\times B_n
\longrightarrow
B_{n+1}.
}
$$

The critical point is that the second step counts **ten already-defined
\(B_n\) landscapes**.

It does not simply return to one hundred independently primitive coins.

# Boundary \(B_{n-1}\): One Coin

At one subordinate peer boundary

$$
B_{n-1,\alpha},
$$

the readable macrostate domain is

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal M_{n-1,\alpha}
=
\{H,T\}.
}
$$

There are two readable distinctions:

$$
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
$$

For this construction, no deeper nontrivial multiplicity landscape is
assigned beneath the individual coin.

The coin is simply the primitive subordinate two-state object used in the
example.

# Boundary \(B_n\): Ten Coins Become One Ensemble

Now let \(B_n\) contain ten peer coin boundaries:

$$
\left\{
B_{n-1,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha=1}^{10}.
$$

One joint realization is

$$
\mu_n
=
\left(
x_{n-1,1},
x_{n-1,2},
\ldots,
x_{n-1,10}
\right),
$$

with

$$
x_{n-1,\alpha}\in\{H,T\}.
$$

The unrestricted formal microstate domain is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\mathfrak M_n
=
\{H,T\}^{10}.
}
$$

There are

$$
2^{10}=1024
$$

formal microstates.

But \(B_n\) does not retain ten separate \(H/T\) macrostate systems.

It introduces a new whole-system classification.

# The New Macrostate

Let

$$
i=N_T
$$

be the number of tails in the ten-coin realization.

Then

$$
i\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\}.
$$

So the readable macrostate domain at \(B_n\) is

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal M_n
=
\{0,1,\ldots,10\}.
}
$$

Ten two-state boundaries have therefore become one eleven-state landscape:

$$
\boxed{
10\times\{H,T\}
\not\equiv
\mathcal M_n.
}
$$

Instead,

$$
\boxed{
\left\{
B_{n-1,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha=1}^{10}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal M_n
=
\{0,\ldots,10\}.
}
$$

This is the first recursive replacement.

[Recursive Replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

# Formal Microstates and Macrostates

Boundary \(B_n\) classifies each formal microstate by its number of tails:

$$
\boxed{
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n.
}
$$

with

$$
\boxed{
\pi_n(\mu_n)
=
N_T(\mu_n).
}
$$

For example,

$$
\mu_n
=
(H,H,T,H,T,T,H,H,T,H)
$$

contains four tails.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\pi_n(\mu_n)=4.
}
$$

Many distinct formal microstates map to the same macrostate.

That many-to-one classification creates multiplicity.

# The Multiplicity Landscape

The multiplicity of macrostate \(i\) is

$$
\boxed{
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|
=
\binom{10}{i}.
}
$$

Its logarithmic coordinate is

$$
\boxed{
S_{n,i}
=
\ln W_{n,i}
=
\ln
\binom{10}{i}.
}
$$

The complete native multiplicity landscape is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal W_n
=
\left\{
\binom{10}{i}
\right\}_{i=0}^{10}.
}
$$

Explicitly,

$$
\mathcal W_n
=
\{1,10,45,120,210,252,210,120,45,10,1\}.
$$

The maximum multiplicity occurs at

$$
i=5.
$$

# Compatible Possibilities Multiply

The ten binary peer domains jointly contain

$$
\boxed{
2^{10}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}2
}
$$

formal possibilities.

This is multiplicative composition.

# Mutually Exclusive Alternatives Add

The whole-system macrostate fibers partition those possibilities:

$$
\boxed{
2^{10}
=
\sum_{i=0}^{10}
\binom{10}{i}.
}
$$

Thus the coin example displays the two primitive count operations directly:

> **Compatible possibilities multiply.**

> **Mutually exclusive alternatives add.**

[Counting Requires Distinguishability →](counting.qmd)

# Realization Does Not Create Multiplicity

Now suppose one particular coin configuration is realized.

The multiplicity landscape does not suddenly appear because that realization
occurred.

Before any particular realization is selected,

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\binom{10}{i}
$$

is already defined by the boundary classification.

For example,

$$
\boxed{
W_{n,0}=1
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
W_{n,5}=252.
}
$$

A subordinate coin transition can change which formal microstate is
realized.

It may also change which macrostate is occupied.

But it does not change either multiplicity.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{subordinate transition}
\longrightarrow
\text{change of realization}
}
$$

but

$$
\boxed{
\text{subordinate transition}
\not\longrightarrow
\text{creation of }W_{n,i}.
}
$$

This is the first major result of the coin construction.

> **The subordinate event realizes the multiplicity landscape.  
> It does not create the multiplicity landscape.**

[Multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

# The Same Transition Changes Meaning With the Boundary

At subordinate peer boundary

$$
B_{n-1,\alpha},
$$

the transition

$$
H_\alpha
\rightarrow
T_\alpha
$$

is a readable macrostate transition.

But relative to \(B_n\), the same event is a transition between formal
microstates:

$$
\mu_n
=
(x_1,\ldots,H_\alpha,\ldots,x_{10})
$$

to

$$
\mu_n'
=
(x_1,\ldots,T_\alpha,\ldots,x_{10}).
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\mu_n
\rightarrow
\mu_n'
}
$$

is a microstate transition relative to \(B_n\).

If the original ensemble contained \(i\) tails, the readable \(B_n\)
consequence is

$$
\boxed{
i
\rightarrow
i+1.
}
$$

But \(B_n\) need not identify which peer coin produced the transition.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{macrostate transition at }B_{n-1,\alpha}
=
\text{microstate transition relative to }B_n.
}
$$

Resolving the individual coin requires changing the count boundary.

[Macrostate and Microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

# Native Direction Within the Ten-Coin Landscape

Consider the adjacent ensemble transition

$$
i\rightarrow i+1.
$$

Its native multiplicity ratio is

$$
\frac{
W_{n,i+1}
}{
W_{n,i}
}
=
\frac{
\binom{10}{i+1}
}{
\binom{10}{i}
}.
$$

Using the binomial identity,

$$
\boxed{
\frac{
W_{n,i+1}
}{
W_{n,i}
}
=
\frac{
10-i
}{
i+1
}.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,i\rightarrow i+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
10-i
}{
i+1
}
\right).
}
$$

For the transition

$$
5\rightarrow6,
$$

we obtain

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,5\rightarrow6}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac56
\right)
<0.
}
$$

So native \(B_n\) multiplicity favors state \(5\) over state \(6\).

Nothing about this calculation refers yet to an enclosing boundary.

# Now Change the Boundary Again

Introduce ten equivalent \(B_n\) landscapes:

$$
\left\{
B_{n,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha=1}^{10}.
$$

Each peer has the state domain

$$
\mathcal M_{n,\alpha}
=
\{0,\ldots,10\}
$$

and multiplicity

$$
W_{n,\alpha,i_\alpha}
=
\binom{10}{i_\alpha}.
$$

The individual \(H/T\) states have already been replaced as the readable
macrostate classification of each \(B_n\) peer.

The objects entering the next recursive composition are therefore:

$$
\boxed{
10\text{ ten-coin landscapes},
}
$$

not

$$
\boxed{
100\text{ independently readable coin states}.
}
$$

This distinction is central.

# The Enclosing State \(J\)

Let the enclosing boundary classify the ten peer macrostates by

$$
\boxed{
J
=
\sum_{\alpha=1}^{10}
i_\alpha.
}
$$

Since each

$$
0\leq i_\alpha\leq10,
$$

we have

$$
J\in\{0,1,\ldots,100\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal M_{n+1}
=
\{0,1,\ldots,100\}.
}
$$

The second recursive replacement is

$$
\boxed{
10\times\mathcal M_n
\longrightarrow
\mathcal M_{n+1}.
}
$$

# Enclosing Multiplicity Is Built Recursively

Take one specific peer-state tuple:

$$
(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_{10}).
$$

The multiplicities of the compatible peer states multiply:

$$
\boxed{
W_{\mathrm{tuple}}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}
W_{n,\alpha,i_\alpha}.
}
$$

For the coin landscapes,

$$
W_{\mathrm{tuple}}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}
\binom{10}{i_\alpha}.
$$

Now fix enclosing state \(J\).

Every mutually exclusive tuple satisfying

$$
i_1+i_2+\cdots+i_{10}=J
$$

belongs to that enclosing classification.

Those alternatives add.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\sum_{
i_1+\cdots+i_{10}=J
}
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}
W_{n,\alpha,i_\alpha}.
}
$$

For the coin ensemble,

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\sum_{
i_1+\cdots+i_{10}=J
}
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}
\binom{10}{i_\alpha}.
}
$$

This is the primitive recursive definition.

# The Familiar Hundred-Coin Result Emerges

The multivariate Vandermonde identity gives

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\binom{100}{J}.
}
$$

This is exactly the same closed-form combinatorial result obtained by
counting \(J\) tails among one hundred binary slots.

But the logical order matters.

R<sup>2</sup>D did not begin \(B_{n+1}\) with one hundred primitive coin
identities.

It began with ten already-defined \(B_n\) landscapes.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recursive composition}
\Rightarrow
\binom{100}{J}
}
$$

does not imply

$$
\boxed{
\binom{100}{J}
\Rightarrow
100\text{ primitive }H/T\text{ objects at }B_{n+1}.
}
$$

This is one of the most important results of the example.

> **Recursive replacement preserves count consequence without preserving
> subordinate state identity.**

[Why R²D Is Not Coarse-Graining →](not-coarse-graining.qmd)

# Total Multiplicity Is Preserved Recursively

The unrestricted multiplicity of each \(B_n\) landscape is

$$
\Theta_n=2^{10}.
$$

Ten such landscapes therefore give

$$
\boxed{
\Theta_{n+1}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{10}
\Theta_{n,\alpha}
=
(2^{10})^{10}
=
2^{100}.
}
$$

Again, the familiar one-hundred-bit count is recovered.

But it is recovered through recursive composition.

# Select One Representative Peer

Now select one \(B_n\) peer, labeled \(\alpha\), and let its local state be

$$
i.
$$

Fix the enclosing state at

$$
J.
$$

Then the other nine peer landscapes must satisfy

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}
i_\beta
=
J-i.
}
$$

This lets us calculate exactly how much enclosing multiplicity is compatible
with one local state.

# Compatible Enclosing Multiplicity

The complete enclosing multiplicity compatible with selected local state
\(i\) is

$$
\Theta_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
W_{n,\alpha,i}
\sum_{
\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}i_\beta=J-i
}
\prod_{\beta\neq\alpha}
W_{n,\beta,i_\beta}.
$$

For the coin landscapes,

$$
\Theta_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\binom{10}{i}
\sum_{
\sum_{\beta\neq\alpha}i_\beta=J-i
}
\prod_{\beta\neq\alpha}
\binom{10}{i_\beta}.
$$

The nine-landscape Vandermonde identity gives

$$
\boxed{
\Theta_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\binom{10}{i}
\binom{90}{J-i}.
}
$$

This is the number of enclosing realizations compatible with the selected
local classification \(i\).

# Enclosing Extension Per Local Possibility

Recall

$$
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}
=
\frac{
\Theta_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}
}{
W_{n,\alpha,i}
}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\binom{90}{J-i}.
}
$$

And the R<sup>2</sup>D possibility coordinate is

$$
\boxed{
P_{n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\binom{90}{J-i}.
}
$$

This makes the meaning of possibility particularly clear.

> **Possibility is not the multiplicity of the local state.**

It is the compatible enclosing extension available **per local possibility**.

[Possibility →](possibility.qmd)

# Why the Ninety Does Not Mean Ninety Primitive Coins

The term

$$
\binom{90}{J-i}
$$

has a familiar closed form.

But within the recursive construction it counts compatible compositions of
the other nine \(B_n\) landscapes.

It should not be interpreted as proof that \(B_{n+1}\) has directly recovered
ninety individually readable coin states.

Again:

> **Closed-form equivalence does not restore subordinate state identity.**

# Large Enclosing Multiplicity Alone Does Not Create Direction

Now remove the restriction to one fixed enclosing state \(J\).

If the other nine \(B_n\) landscapes are unrestricted, each selected local
state has the same amount of compatible enclosing extension:

$$
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}
=
\prod_{\beta\neq\alpha}
\Theta_{n,\beta}.
$$

Since

$$
\Theta_{n,\beta}=2^{10},
$$

we obtain

$$
\boxed{
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}
=
(2^{10})^9
=
2^{90}
}
$$

for every \(i\).

Therefore,

$$
P_{n,\alpha,i}
=
90\ln2
$$

for every \(i\), and consequently

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}=0.
}
$$

This gives an important exact result:

> **Large enclosing multiplicity is not sufficient for direction.**

Direction requires **unequal** enclosing compatibility.

# Directional Possibility Under Fixed \(J\)

Return to a fixed enclosing state \(J\).

For

$$
i\rightarrow i+1,
$$

directional possibility is

$$
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i+1}^{(J)}
}{
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
}
\right).
$$

Substituting the exact extension multiplicities,

$$
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\left[
\frac{
\binom{90}{J-i-1}
}{
\binom{90}{J-i}
}
\right].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
J-i
}{
91-J+i
}
\right).
}
$$

This is an exact enclosing-defined directional count relation.

No occupancy postulate has been used.

No probability has been introduced.

# Enclosing Compatibility Can Reverse Native Direction

Now take the explicit transition

$$
5\rightarrow6.
$$

The native multiplicity relation is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{5\rightarrow6}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac56
\right)
\approx
-0.1823.
}
$$

Native multiplicity favors state \(5\).

Now choose the enclosing state

$$
J=60.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{5\rightarrow6}^{(60)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\right)
\approx
0.4238.
}
$$

Enclosing compatibility favors state \(6\).

The complete compatible-count difference is therefore

$$
\Delta S+\Delta P
=
\ln
\left(
\frac56
\right)
+
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\right).
$$

So

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S+\Delta P
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{275}{216}
\right)
\approx
0.2415
>0.
}
$$

The net compatible count now favors \(6\).

But nothing about the native landscape

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\binom{10}{i}
$$

has changed.

Only the enclosing compatibility relation changed.

# This Is the Exact Top-Down Result

The coin construction therefore proves:

$$
\boxed{
\text{same local multiplicity landscape}
+
\text{different enclosing compatibility}
\rightarrow
\text{different local directional support}.
}
$$

More strongly, the enclosing relation can:

- create direction;
- cancel native direction;
- or reverse native direction.

The subordinate transition does not define the relation capable of doing
this.

This is the second major exact result of the example.

# Reconstructing the Enclosing State

The compatibility fibers associated with one selected peer partition the
fixed enclosing macrostate.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\sum_i
\Theta_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}.
}
$$

For the coin construction,

$$
\boxed{
\binom{100}{J}
=
\sum_i
\binom{10}{i}
\binom{90}{J-i}.
}
$$

Since

$$
e^{P_{n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}}
=
\binom{90}{J-i},
$$

the same relation can be written

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\sum_i
W_{n,i}
e^{P_{n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}}.
}
$$

This equation makes the recursive architecture visible:

> **The enclosing multiplicity is reconstructed from local multiplicity
> multiplied by compatible enclosing extension.**

# What Is Exact So Far?

Everything up to this point follows from finite combinatorics once the
boundaries and classification maps have been defined.

We have not yet needed:

$$
\Delta R,
$$

$$
\Delta A,
$$

$$
\Delta G,
$$

the R<sup>2</sup>D law,

or the R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law.

That separation matters.

The combinatorics establish the count architecture.

The next step introduces R<sup>2</sup>D realization postulates.

# Add Productive Constraint

Return to

$$
5\rightarrow6
$$

under

$$
J=60.
$$

Choose a unit distinguishability for the example:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{n,5\rightarrow6}=1.
}
$$

Let the productive component of enclosing constraint be

$$
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}\geq0.
$$

Retention is then

$$
\Delta R_{n,5\rightarrow6}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n,5\rightarrow6}.
$$

So

$$
\boxed{
\Delta R_{n,5\rightarrow6}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}.
}
$$

The local asymmetry is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,5\rightarrow6}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\right)
-
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}.
}
$$

[Constraint and Retention →](constraint-retention.qmd)

# Now the Occupancy Postulate Enters

R<sup>2</sup>D postulates

$$
\Delta G
=
\Delta\tau+\Delta A.
$$

Under proportional occurrence realization,

$$
\Delta\tau
\approx
\Delta S.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta G_{5\rightarrow6}
\approx
\Delta S_{5\rightarrow6}
+
\Delta P_{5\rightarrow6}^{(60)}
-
\Delta R_{5\rightarrow6}.
$$

Substituting the exact coin counts,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta G_{5\rightarrow6}
\approx
\ln
\left(
\frac{275}{216}
\right)
-
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}.
}
$$

Exponentiating gives the predicted occupancy ratio

$$
\boxed{
\frac{c_{n,6}}{c_{n,5}}
\approx
\frac{275}{216}
e^{-C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}}.
}
$$

This result contains two logically different ingredients.

The factor

$$
\frac{275}{216}
$$

comes from exact combinatorics.

The mapping from that count bias into realized occupancy is an
R<sup>2</sup>D realization postulate.

[Occupancy and Occurrence →](occupancy-occurrence.qmd)

# Constraint Can Cancel the Enclosing Bias

At the mode-exchange condition,

$$
\Delta G\approx0.
$$

For this example that occurs when

$$
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\approx
\ln
\left(
\frac{275}{216}
\right).
$$

Then the enclosing-compatible count bias is completely balanced by productive
retention.

This is a concrete realization of the general architecture

$$
\boxed{
\text{multiplicity}
+
\text{possibility}
-
\text{retention}
\rightarrow
\text{occupancy}.
}
$$

# Closure Can Be Exact Locally but Asymmetric Enclosingly

Now consider the local return

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}:
5\rightarrow6\rightarrow5.
}
$$

Let the forward transition occur while the enclosing state is

$$
J_H=60.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_H
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\right).
}
$$

Let the return transition occur under a different enclosing state,

$$
J_L=40.
$$

For

$$
6\rightarrow5,
$$

the enclosing possibility is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_L
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{56}{35}
\right).
}
$$

Therefore the possibility accumulated around the local closure is

$$
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_H+\Delta P_L.
$$

So

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\frac{56}{35}
\right)
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{154}{63}
\right)
>0.
}
$$

# Native Multiplicity Still Closes Exactly

The native multiplicity coordinate gives

$$
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac56
\right)
+
\ln
\left(
\frac65
\right).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0.
}
$$

So the same cycle satisfies

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}>0.
}
$$

This is exact combinatorics.

> **The local multiplicity path closes.  
> The enclosing compatibility relation need not.**

[Closure →](closure.qmd)

# Why This Is Not a Contradiction

The two quantities describe different relations.

$$
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}
$$

belongs to the native local multiplicity landscape.

$$
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}
$$

belongs to the changing enclosing compatibility relation.

The local state returns.

But the forward and return legs do not have to occur under reciprocal
enclosing conditions.

This is the primitive architecture of asymmetric closure.

# Closure Asymmetry Requires Retention Too

If productive retention is also specified around the closure, define

$$
\boxed{
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\sum_{\chi\in\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}}
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\chi}.
}
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
-
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
$$

The coin combinatorics alone do not determine

$$
\Delta R_{\mathcal C}
$$

or

$$
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}.
$$

Those require the additional R<sup>2</sup>D constraint and realization
architecture.

[Asymmetry →](asymmetry.qmd)

# An Open Enclosing Path Organizes Every Equivalent Peer

Now suppose the enclosing state follows an open path:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal O_{n+1}:
J_0
\rightarrow
J_1
\rightarrow
\cdots
\rightarrow
J_m,
}
$$

with

$$
J_m\neq J_0.
$$

For local transition

$$
i\rightarrow i+1,
$$

each enclosing state \(J_r\) defines

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J_r)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
J_r-i
}{
91-J_r+i
}
\right).
}
$$

For example, with

$$
i=5
$$

and enclosing path

$$
60\rightarrow61\rightarrow62,
$$

we obtain

$$
\Delta P(60)
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{55}{36}
\right),
$$

$$
\Delta P(61)
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{56}{35}
\right),
$$

and

$$
\Delta P(62)
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{57}{34}
\right).
$$

As the enclosing state changes, the directional possibility acting on the
same local alternative changes.

# Equivalent Peers Receive the Same Enclosing Relation

Because the ten \(B_n\) landscapes are equivalent under the enclosing
classification,

$$
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
K_{n+1|n,\beta,i}^{(J)}
$$

for equivalent peers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\Delta P_{n,\beta,i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}.
}
$$

One enclosing compatibility relation simultaneously defines the same
directional possibility for every equivalent peer.

The peers do not have to communicate this organization laterally.

They share the same enclosing relation.

This is the mathematical core of the top-down architecture.

# The Causal Proposal Comes After the Combinatorics

The exact combinatorics establish that the enclosing relation defines which
local alternatives have greater compatible extension.

R<sup>2</sup>D then makes the stronger causal proposal:

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\left\{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right\}_{\alpha=1}^{10}.
}
$$

For one representative peer,

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
}
$$

The enclosing occurrence defines its compatible local realization.

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

# Recursive Carry Points the Other Way — But Is Not Causal

Once the local closure is completed, changing the count boundary reclassifies
it:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
$$

This arrow does not mean

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\Longrightarrow
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

The two relations answer different questions.

Causal realization:

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
}
$$

Recursive readout:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
$$

[Recursive Carry →](recursive-carry.qmd)

# Realization Adds Three More Count Relations

The static coin construction defines multiplicity exactly.

Once realized occurrence is introduced, three additional quantities must be
kept separate.

## State occurrence

$$
\Delta\tau_{n,i\rightarrow k}
$$

compares occurrence counts associated with two states.

## Opposed-leg nonreciprocity

$$
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
$$

compares complete realizations of the two opposed closure legs.

## Across-boundary recurrence

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
$$

compares how often the local closure and enclosing transition recur.

These are not interchangeable.

# Opposed Closure Legs

Let

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
$$

count complete realizations of one oriented closure leg and

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
$$

count complete realizations of its opposed leg.

Define

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
},
\qquad
0<\eta\leq1.
}
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
-\ln\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}
\right).
}
$$

This is occurrence nonreciprocity.

It is not closure recurrence.

# Closure Recurrence Is Separate

Within a recurrence-comparison domain \(\mathcal D_R\), define

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

as the number of local closure recurrences and

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
$$

as the number of corresponding enclosing recurrences.

Then

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\chi_{n+1})
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha})
}.
}
$$

The static coin combinatorics do not determine \(\rho\).

It belongs to realized recurrence.

[Recurrence →](recurrence.qmd)

# The Finite-Count Efficiency Postulate

The Canon introduces a separate R<sup>2</sup>D realization postulate for
finite opposed-leg counts.

Let

$$
N_i>0,
\qquad
N_k>0.
$$

Define

$$
\boxed{
\epsilon_H
=
\frac{
N_i
}{
N_k+1
}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\epsilon_L
=
\frac{
N_k
}{
N_i+1
}.
}
$$

Their product is

$$
\boxed{
\epsilon_H\epsilon_L
=
\frac{
N_iN_k
}{
(N_i+1)(N_k+1)
}.
}
$$

For finite positive counts,

$$
\boxed{
0<
\epsilon_H\epsilon_L
<1.
}
$$

That inequality is mathematical.

R<sup>2</sup>D then postulates the realization relation

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\epsilon_H\epsilon_L.
}
$$

The identification of the mathematical finite-count product with physical
directional realization efficiency is therefore a postulate, not a
combinatorial theorem.

# A Symmetric Finite Example

Take

$$
N_i=N_k=5.
$$

Then

$$
\epsilon_H
=
\epsilon_L
=
\frac56.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\eta
=
\frac{25}{36}.
}
$$

The corresponding occurrence-count loss is

$$
\boxed{
L_\tau
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{36}{25}
\right).
}
$$

# The Second-Law Readout

The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law postulates

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
$$

For this finite example,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{36}{25}
\right).
}
$$

If

$$
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
b_{n+1}^{+}
}{
b_{n+1}^{-}
}
\right),
$$

then

$$
\boxed{
\frac{
b_{n+1}^{+}
}{
b_{n+1}^{-}
}
=
\frac{36}{25}.
}
$$

The local reading is

$$
\eta
=
\frac{25}{36},
$$

while the enclosing background read is its reciprocal count ratio:

$$
\frac{
b_{n+1}^{+}
}{
b_{n+1}^{-}
}
=
\frac{36}{25}.
$$

No count needs to be destroyed or transported upward.

These are two boundary-specific logarithmic readings connected by the
Second-Law postulate.

[The R²D Second Law →](second-law.qmd)

# What the Coins Prove Exactly

The coin construction establishes several results without any physical
R<sup>2</sup>D realization postulate.

### 1. Boundary change creates a new state classification

At \(B_n\),

$$
\mathcal M_n
=
\{0,\ldots,10\}.
$$

At \(B_{n+1}\),

$$
\mathcal M_{n+1}
=
\{0,\ldots,100\}.
$$

These are different state domains.

### 2. Subordinate realization does not create multiplicity

A coin transition changes realization.

It does not create

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\binom{10}{i}.
$$

### 3. Recursive replacement preserves multiplicity consequence

The recursively composed enclosing landscape satisfies

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\binom{100}{J}.
}
$$

But this does not restore one hundred subordinate coin identities as
primitive states at \(B_{n+1}\).

### 4. Uniform enclosing compatibility creates no directional possibility

If every local state has the same compatible enclosing extension,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P=0.
}
$$

### 5. Unequal enclosing compatibility creates directional possibility

For fixed \(J\),

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
J-i
}{
91-J+i
}
\right).
}
$$

### 6. Enclosing compatibility can reverse native local bias

For

$$
5\rightarrow6
$$

under

$$
J=60,
$$

$$
\Delta S<0,
$$

while

$$
\Delta P>0
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S+\Delta P>0.
}
$$

The native landscape has not changed.

### 7. Local multiplicity can close while enclosing possibility does not

For

$$
5\rightarrow6\rightarrow5
$$

under different enclosing conditions,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{\mathcal C}>0.
}
$$

These are exact mathematical results.

# What the Coins Do Not Prove by Themselves

The static combinatorics do **not** establish

$$
\boxed{
\Delta G
=
\Delta\tau+\Delta A.
}
$$

They do not establish proportional occurrence realization,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\tau\approx\Delta S.
}
$$

They do not establish the finite-count realization postulate,

$$
\boxed{
\eta
=
\epsilon_H\epsilon_L.
}
$$

They do not establish the R<sup>2</sup>D law,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}
=
C_{n+1}
\lambda_{n+1}
\rho_{n+1|n}.
}
$$

And they do not establish the R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_\tau.
}
$$

Those are R<sup>2</sup>D realization propositions applied to the exact
recursive count architecture.

This distinction between **theorem** and **postulate** is essential.

# What the Coins Establish About Causal Agency

The exact construction does establish something stronger than ordinary
statistical correlation.

A subordinate transition cannot be the origin of the multiplicity landscape
whose occupancy it changes.

That landscape is already defined by the boundary classification.

Likewise, a \(B_n\) transition cannot by itself define the \(B_{n+1}\)
compatibility relation that can reverse the directional significance of that
transition.

Thus:

> **The local event realizes structure that it does not generate.**

R<sup>2</sup>D adds the causal proposal that the enclosing relation is
causally prior to the compatible subordinate realization.

That stronger statement remains a testable part of the R<sup>2</sup>D
program.

# The Entire Example in One View

The recursion begins with ten binary peers:

$$
\boxed{
10\times\{H,T\}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal M_n=\{0,\ldots,10\}.
}
$$

Their multiplicity landscape is

$$
\boxed{
W_{n,i}
=
\binom{10}{i}.
}
$$

Ten such landscapes recursively compose:

$$
\boxed{
10\times\mathcal M_n
\longrightarrow
\mathcal M_{n+1}
=
\{0,\ldots,100\}.
}
$$

Their enclosing multiplicity is

$$
\boxed{
W_{n+1,J}
=
\sum_{
\sum_\alpha i_\alpha=J
}
\prod_\alpha
W_{n,\alpha,i_\alpha}
=
\binom{100}{J}.
}
$$

For one selected peer,

$$
\boxed{
K_{n+1|n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\binom{90}{J-i},
}
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
P_{n,\alpha,i}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\binom{90}{J-i}.
}
$$

Direction is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta P_{i\rightarrow i+1}^{(J)}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
J-i
}{
91-J+i
}
\right).
}
$$

Thus the complete architecture appears:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{subordinate states}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{new boundary classification}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{native multiplicity}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{recursive composition}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{enclosing compatibility}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{directional possibility}
\end{array}
}
$$

Only after this exact structure is established are constraint, occupancy,
recurrence, the R<sup>2</sup>D law, and the Second Law added as realization
relations.

# The Key Lesson

The coin example reduces R<sup>2</sup>D to finite arithmetic.

It shows that:

> **The boundary defines the possible structure.**

> **Subordinate events realize that structure; they do not create it.**

> **Changing the boundary replaces state identity while preserving
> multiplicity consequence.**

> **The enclosing compatibility relation can change or reverse local
> directional support without changing the native local landscape.**

And that leads to the core causal question of R<sup>2</sup>D:

> **Have we mistaken the mechanism that realizes a state for the relation
> that organizes which state is favored?**
